section_summary: This section concludes one draft statement on postwar economic policy toward Japan, then presents internal critiques, an outline, and a fuller policy paper covering occupation, reparations, economic disarmament, internal reform, and Japan’s eventual integration into world trade. Later memoranda debate whether broad long-term policy was yet useful and propose concrete research on Japanese industry, shipping, overseas assets, subsistence, and reparations; field correspondence from New Delhi discusses intelligence staffing and Japanese supplies of petroleum coke and iron ore. The section also contains a cross-reference sheet, correspondence between Mrs. Fred L. Cagwin and Joseph C. Grew about Japan’s postwar future and Christianity, and the opening of Elizabeth Schumpeter’s study advocating a relatively liberal economic settlement in light of Japan’s population and limited resources.

subfiles.title: Economic Policy Toward Japan: Summary Statement
subfiles.about: The concluding sections prescribe controls over Japan’s war potential and internal economy while envisioning its eventual integration into an open world economy.
subfiles.summary: The paper recommends removing or converting war-related plants, restricting imports of strategic materials, and ending subsidies or other devices that sustain uneconomic industries tied to military self-sufficiency. It calls for reform of large corporations, banking, and labor conditions during a relatively short period of control, followed by equal access to international trade and rejection of Japanese-controlled economic blocs.

subfiles.title: Memorandum commenting on “Economic Policy Toward Japan: Summary Statement”
subfiles.about: The memorandum praises the draft but argues that it understates the domestic and international role of Japanese monopolistic concerns.
subfiles.summary: Memo praises the draft 'Economic Policy Toward Japan' as comprehensive and urges fuller treatment of monopolies like Mitsui and Mitsubishi in Thailand as instruments of war preparation, comparable to I. G. Farben.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Economic Policy Toward Japan
subfiles.about: Lockhart explains the political assumptions behind the attached economic-policy paper and warns that major changes in those assumptions would require extensive rewriting.
subfiles.summary: Memo says the paper parallels a German-policy document, rests on the Atlantic Charter, and argues defeat and occupation may favor peaceful integration, though unsettled high-level policy could require changes.

subfiles.title: Outline of Economic Policy Toward Japan
subfiles.about: This outline lists the sections and principal arguments of a proposed policy paper on Japan’s postwar economy.
subfiles.summary: The outline covers the foreign-policy background, Cairo decisions, general objectives, three postwar periods, a minimum economy, restitution and reparations, and control of the war potential. It concludes with proposed reforms of Japanese corporations, banking, and labor and the gradual integration of Japan into a free world economy.

subfiles.title: Economic Policy Toward Japan
subfiles.about: The paper presents a comprehensive American program for Japan’s economy from surrender and occupation through long-term reintegration into peaceful international commerce.
subfiles.summary: It connects economic policy to enduring peace, the Open Door, the Atlantic Charter, and the Cairo decisions, proposing three stages: military occupation, close economic control, and gradual integration into a free world economy. The paper addresses emergency relief, transportation and finance, restitution, reparations limited by minimum living standards and essential imports, expropriation of major overseas holdings, and controls on strategic industries and materials. It also calls for reform of concentrated corporate and financial power, broader credit for small enterprises, an effective labor movement, and equal but non-discriminatory participation by Japan in world trade.

subfiles.title: Comments on the Paper on Economic Policy Toward Japan
subfiles.about: Blakeslee offers editorial and substantive comments on the policy paper after reading it twice.
subfiles.summary: Comments find the paper consistent with the Area Committee on the Far East; suggests statistical support, answering Moulton, clarifying a minimum economy, reconsidering foregoing reparations, and mentioning agrarian reform.

subfiles.title: Character of Immediate Work to Be Done on Economic Treatment of Japan and Japanese Reparations
subfiles.about: Luthringer recommends postponing a broad policy statement and formal reparations committee in favor of targeted analytical studies.
subfiles.summary: He argues that uncertain high-level policy toward Germany makes an abstract long-term statement on Japan premature and likely to invite misunderstanding. Proposed studies would examine the loss of Japan’s empire, destruction of heavy industry, restrictions on shipping and aviation, effects on national income and subsistence, reparations from output or seized equipment, overseas assets, transfers to China, and the personnel required for economic control. A small steering committee would guide this work before any formal reparations or economic-disarmament committee was created.

subfiles.title: Supply and Resources
subfiles.about: Corry forwards letters to Johnstone and Hewlett and requests Washington analysis of Japanese aluminum and iron-resource questions.
subfiles.summary: Corry asks for a memorandum on how interruption of petroleum-coke supplies from Netherlands East Indies refineries would affect the Japanese economy and aluminum production. He also summarizes Dyott’s view that Japanese production of iron from pyritic residues was already included in a substantially higher estimate of domestic ore supply.

subfiles.title: Letter to Paul H. Johnstone
subfiles.about: Corry reports action on Johnstone’s instructions concerning McCune’s return to Kandy and gives brief news from the New Delhi office.
subfiles.summary: Corry tells Johnstone his letters go to Hewlett, a cable favored delaying McCune's return until Meiklejohn's arrival at Chongqing, and reports a generals' inspection and an upcoming meeting.

subfiles.title: Letter to Gregory Hewlett
subfiles.about: Corry reports on personnel, intelligence distribution, biological-warfare collection, and travel in the China–Burma–India theater.
subfiles.summary: Corry to Hewlett: cable advises McCune stay until Meiklejohn relieves him; intelligence on transport and ports; staffing and travel, a G-2 briefing on biological warfare and his Kashmir trip.

subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Note: Appointment of an Executive Committee of the Joint Conference Committee
subfiles.about: The sheet directs the reader to the original letter concerning appointment of an executive committee.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: November 30, 1944 letter on appointing an Executive Committee of the Joint Conference Committee (840.50/11-3044).

subfiles.title: Letter asking about Japan’s collapse, comeback, and Christianity
subfiles.about: Mrs. Cagwin seeks guidance for a club paper on whether Japan’s collapse or recovery would pose the greater postwar danger and asks about Christianity’s future in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Mrs. Cagwin, drawing on Methodist missions and her son's Pacific service, asks about economic collapse, renewed Japanese power, communism and Christianity, arguing against treating all Japanese as irredeemable and asking about Kagawa.

subfiles.title: Reply to Mrs. Fred L. Cagwin
subfiles.about: Grew responds to Mrs. Cagwin by recommending speeches, publications, research organizations, and a missionary expert rather than attempting a short substantive answer.
subfiles.summary: Grew says her questions are too complex for a letter, encloses three speeches, and recommends the Council on Foreign Relations, Foreign Policy Association, Carnegie Endowment, IPR, Foreign Relations volumes and Joe Mickle.

subfiles.title: The Postwar Treatment of Japan
subfiles.to: Economic and Financial Group, Council on Foreign Relations
subfiles.about: Schumpeter reviews arguments for liberal economic treatment of defeated Japan and begins a demographic and resource analysis.
subfiles.summary: Drawing chiefly on the Princeton conference report, Harold G. Moulton and Louis Marlio, and Sir George Sansom, Schumpeter argues that a defeated and disarmed Japan would still need industry, international trade, a merchant marine, and eventual participation in international economic arrangements. She contrasts that position with proposals to eliminate heavy industry or reduce Japan to agriculture and stresses the administrative difficulties of extensive economic control. Population statistics for Japan, Korea, Taiwan, Manchuria, and comparator countries support her contention that the densely populated home islands could not subsist on agriculture alone and would probably continue to experience population growth.
